Estimating a high-dimensional classification task using regression relies heavily on feature selection to mitigate the negative effects of excessive data dimensionality. This paper introduces LapPPe, a projection-based two-stage estimation technique that projects data through a linear layer, retains only projected components expected to carry meaningful information, and then executes a classification task using the transformed features. In the regression paradigm, this method prevents dimensionality-induced overfitting while offering extensive flexibility. To adapt it for classification, we derive a classification-specific loss function through careful theoretical analysis and demonstrate its efficacy by adapting popular estimators. Extensive numerical evaluations across real- and synthetic datasets indicate that the proposed method substantially improves predictive accuracy in high-dimensional settings compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches.

While classifiers have long been established components of the computer vision pipeline, recent years have seen the community explore optimizing them. However, assuming such improvements occur within a vacuum ignores potential risks under adversarial conditions. This paper investigates classifiers within a synthetic, 2-dimensional Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) setting. Our results demonstrate an attack methodology where a malicious algorithm, intervening between an image generator and a classifier, subtly alters inputs to gradually bias the classifier toward any arbitrary target class. Unlike standard adversarial perturbations introduced post-hoc, this MITM assault is inherently position-dependent. Consequently, assuming no protection exists against this specific vector, any classifier that is accessible via an imperfect generator becomes fully subvertable in an iterative, gradient-based manner, as seen in prior research.

Consequently, effective climate change communication must adopt robust strategies to counteract the widespread impact of online misinformation.

We explore a flat universe within the lattice cosmological framework, specifically focusing on a $Z_2$ gauge theory that couples with simple scalar fields. Our results demonstrate that the scalar fields' interaction with gravity causes the effective cosmological constant to decrease as the epoch progresses into the late stages, analogous to mechanisms proposed in superpotential or spontaneous breaking scenarios. We validate this finding through effective field power spectrum analysis and explicit numerical simulations. Additionally, we perform an explicit calculation of the late-stage Friedmann equation's expansion, which reveals that the model can inherently support flat geometry without requiring an external cosmological constant.

Image segmentation is a fundamental task within image processing that has been the focus of various existing methods, including those based on level sets and active contours. In contrast, this study introduces a novel variational model for image segmentation that integrates four key components: total variation (TV) norms, the curvature of level sets, Gaussian curvature, along with both an intra- and inter-level smoothing term. Although adding these curvature-related terms increases computational cost during segmentation—a challenge addressed by proposing an efficient level set evolution algorithm with guaranteed convergence—our results demonstrate the model's superior performance. Conducted experiments on numerous tests reveal that the proposed approach effectively handles tasks such as segments with sharp intensity changes, loss of details, noise, and irregular structures, yielding highly precise and smooth segments.

The IEEE 802.11p standard facilitates intelligent transportation systems by enabling on-board units to exchange information regarding vehicle position, speed, and status through a Channel State Information (CSI) matrix that evolves over time as traffic conditions change. Results indicate that this method surpasses pure LSTMs, as well as other leading algorithms in terms of both accuracy and efficiency when handling live streaming 802.11p data.

The underpinning theorem for neural networks, the Universal Approximation Theorem, suggests that an appropriately weight-adjusted piecewise continuous function can mimic any other continuous function. This research focuses on the challenge of developing open, scalable cognitive architectures designed for large-scale multi-agent systems engaged in HRC learning. An increasingly significant obstacle in Monte Carlo simulations of fermionic quantum systems is the "sign problem." Knowledge distillation has become a strategy for deploying cost-effectively smaller models by transferring the learned behavior of a large teacher. However, achieving competitive accuracy with a distilled model often necessitates an enormous quantity of training resources. To generate datasets of this magnitude, we introduce Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE), a novel knowledge distillation framework designed specifically for multi-instructor labeled distillation. PILE generates enhanced training data by applying successive student models iteratively to input data. The framework begins by creating a initial ensemble of these students and then refines it through several generations of iterative pairwise comparisons, significantly improving the quality of the distilled knowledge. When applied to image recognition tasks, a PILE-derived dataset enables a distilled model to reach 79.47% top-1 accuracy, a level just 0.5% below that of its four teacher models. Compared to an unsupervised model with the identical computational budget, a PILE model achieves a 7.12 percentage-point boost in top-1 accuracy.

The success of the biological world relies on genetic diversity, nature capitalizing on it to foster the optimization of traits for survival, and addressing how phenotypic diversity functions within Multi-Objective Optimization problems—a rarely explored aspect of biology—is crucial for understanding how genetic diversity supports optimization. This research examines the association between visual phenotype diversity within a population and the relatedness of the individuals (measured by the Hamming distance of their decision-maker vectors) for solving specific "Many Objective Knapsack Problems." It is hypothesized that higher similarity among members of a population, or greater genetic uniformity, results in increased phenotypic diversity. This exploration evaluates many-objective knapsack problems where each additional item adds five new traits, analyzed using two specific methods: (1) a "Many-Objective Knapsack Problem" and, (2) "Many-Objective Knapsack Problem with Constraints." It further evaluates this correlation using the PLS and NSGA-II algorithms. The findings indicate an relationship where the decision-maker vectors' genetic uniformity among individuals within the Pareto set significantly increases diversity in observed phenotypes.

Stable matching problems are central to research in operations research and have broad real-world applications. This paper addresses a variation known as the Three-Dimensional Stable Roommates Challenge, where $3n$ agents are paired into teams of three. Distinguishing himself, each agent values teams based on interpersonal preferences for two partners. We investigate the impact of diverse electron-phonon coupling mechanisms, specifically strain, flexoelectricity, and polarization, on valley physics in two-dimensional materials, employing the rigorous framework of the quantum, coherent, polariton theory of motion. We explicitly derive the expressions of these physical influences, demonstrating how they drive distinct movements along the transversal charge and neutral trajectories, as well as the inter-orbital transitions, thereby deepening the understanding of valley dynamics in system-specific contexts.

The paper proposes the design, analysis, simulation, and experimental verification of an mm-wave microstrip array featuring both high bandwidth and an extensive scanning range. The 2×2 arrangement consists of fractional exponential Bessel functions that enable broad operational bandwidth. Each element measures 30×30 mm² and is engineered to maintain a constant phase over an area approximately 0.7λ by (0.5 to 0.55)λ within the 28–40 GHz band while sustaining variable phase across beyond 0.8λ in both dimensions across that spectrum. The reflector effect results in substantial gain enhancement up through 40 GHz. Measurement and analysis in comparison to simulated data show consistent results across the frequency range of 28–40 GHz. The combination of wide coverage from the specific element pattern and null performance at peripheral angles yields exceptional operational bandwidth. Additionally, the array factor coupled with the generated radiation pattern of the array element produces robust 3-dB isotropic power gain across more than 120 degrees observed experimentally.

Stable quantum computation requires fault tolerance to safeguard against noise that could invalidate outcomes. We introduce two reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms—deep reinforcement learning (DRQL) and multi-agent RL (MRQL)—to iteratively derive fault-tolerant quanta circuit layers capable of performing noisy single-qubit and entangling gate operations.
DRQL has been applied to construct fault-tolerant circuits addressing the 27-qubit surface code, involving single-qubit (X, Z, or CNOT) and one- or two-qubit gates, driven by a Qiskit-based quantum circuit framework and a NASA-developed Markovian noise model tailored for these scenarios.
MRCL, utilizing multiple RL agents, was developed to mitigate resource constraints associated with an excessively large action space in DRQL.
We evaluated the performance and efficiency of both methodologies, finding that MRCL outperforms DRCL within a constrained computational budget by delivering superior success probabilities at shorter circuit depths.
Notably, both algorithms significantly surpass the benchmark representing a naive, baseline circuit approach.
Ultimately, these findings suggest that machine learning techniques can effectively tackle complex, fault-tolerant circuit design challenges, a domain that is otherwise difficult to resolve.

We investigate precision limits when estimating a cavity field's coupling constant using measurements performed on an ancilla. This introduces a quantum metrology instance wherein the primary system is a two-cavity setup, and the ancilla operates across the system-wide ground state. The study demonstrates that the optimal interaction between the ancilla and field generates a quantum excursion—referred to as a "quantum leap"—within the ancilla. We conduct a thorough analysis of the necessary conditions, including the interaction Hamiltonian, coupling parameters, and evolution time. The findings indicate that the information gained allows the precision to reach the Heisenberg limit regarding the coupling constant estimation. Furthermore, the quantum nature of this quantum excursion is what drives this improvement in precision beyond standard strategies. We also show that the achieved precision scales effectively, surviving even under conditions of ancilla initial state impurity.

In financial time-series prediction, discriminating between assets allows for wealth accumulation. This study introduces a new feature engineering methodology designed to simultaneously maximize wealth returns and ensure sufficient model generalization and revenue stability, addressing the inherent challenges in optimizing this trade-off. By leveraging extensive quantitative experience, the proposed approach integrates multiple anti-overfitting strategies—such as early stopping, data augmentation, and regularization—into a coherent feature selection framework that successfully mitigates the generalization-to-performance dilemma, thereby enhancing overall performance. The formation processes governing stellar populations in proto-galaxies during the early universe remain poorly understood. Theories suggest the primordial counterparts of modern star-forming and quiescent galaxies may have hosted nuclear star clusters (NCCs)—dense nuclear star clusters similar in structure to those found in modern systems. Our analysis indicates that although NCCs were once more massive, only a small percentage of binaries were expected to surpass the minimum detection threshold for a signal. Even so, the overall population within these early clusters may simply have been too numerous despite this lower proportion. This study introduces a physics-based modeling approach for semiconductor devices, specifically targeting dual-domain ferroelectric FETs (FETs). The model addresses dual-domain nucleation at the center of the channel and incorporates the impact of domain walls on electrical properties like capacitance and transport. This framework simultaneously solves coupled equations for the electro kinetic state, domain evolution, and transport phenomena to explicitly account for the physics occurring at domain walls. To demonstrate the model's validity regarding the unique dual-region hysteresis and the anomalous capacitive behavior, we simulated an FET with a Si body and SiO2 gate dielectric.
